tags: AI/ML for ADMET and toxicity property prediction — cheminformatics, computational safety pharmacology, model calibration and applicability domain
text: [BLOCKER] The entire "In Silico ADMET & Safety" layer is 25 hardcoded prose strings — there is no model, no descriptor calculation, no data source, and no computation of any kind — Every safety number in the platform is a string literal typed into a JavaScript array. I traced the data flow end to end: `drug.safety` is written at 25 places and read at exactly one (app.js:640), where it is pasted verbatim into the modal HTML. Nothing parses it, derives it, or checks it. A repo-wide grep for any ADMET machinery returned zero hits outside the section heading itself: no `rdkit`, `chemprop`, `deepchem`, `sklearn`, `xgboost`, no `fetch`/`XMLHttpRequest`/API call, no descriptor code, no `Math.random`, no model file, no training data, no reference dataset. The repo's only non-UI files are README.md, app.js, index.html, styles.css and a memory spec. The distribution of the literals betrays their origin: 25/25 rows carry the identical hERG value (24x "hERG IC50 > 50 μM", 1x the same value with "(0% Cardiotoxicity)" appended); Seizure Index appears in 21/25 rows and takes only 3 distinct values {0.00 (9x), 0.01 (8x), 0.02 (4x)}; and the third endpoint slot uses 22 different, mutually incomparable labels across 25 rows. No predictive model produces a point-identical value for 25 chemically distinct entities. Consequence: README.md:98 states "All 25 candidates underwent rigorous computational safety screening" and README.md:96 titles the section "In Silico ADMET & Safety Risk Profile Assessment". Both are false as written: no screening of any kind was performed. A reader — a collaborator, a reviewer, an investor, a student — is being told that a computational safety assessment exists and returned clean results. It does not exist. Every downstream finding in this review is a consequence of this one: the platform's central ADMET claim has no referent. In a therapeutics context this is the failure mode that gets programs killed and reputations destroyed, because the numbers are specific enough (0.01, 4.2%, 50 μM, 99.5/100) to be quoted by someone who assumes they came from somewhere.

text: Required fix for AIML-01: Delete every hardcoded `safety:` string and README.md:96-102 immediately, or replace the section body with an explicit banner: "Illustrative placeholder values. No ADMET model has been run. Not for decision-making." To make the claim real: (1) commit a script (`admet/run.py`) that reads structures from a manifest and calls a named model; (2) for the small-molecule warheads, run ADMET-AI or Chemprop v2 and emit JSON per compound with prediction, uncertainty and AD flag; (3) for the peptide conjugates, run the peptide-appropriate panel (see AIML-06/07) — hERG is not it; (4) write model name, version, training set, date and git SHA into every output record; (5) have app.js read that JSON rather than literals, and render "not assessed" where the pipeline produced nothing.

tags: AI/ML for ADMET and toxicity property prediction — cheminformatics, computational safety pharmacology, model calibration and applicability domain
text: Ground truth for AIML-01: An in-silico ADMET assessment is a reproducible artifact: input structures (SMILES/sequence), a named model with a training set and a published validation, per-prediction output with uncertainty, an applicability-domain verdict, a version, and a timestamp. ADMET-AI (Swanson et al., Bioinformatics 2024, PMID 38913862) is the current open reference implementation for small molecules — Chemprop D-MPNN models trained on the 22 TDC ADMET datasets, runnable locally, emitting per-endpoint predictions plus a percentile against a DrugBank reference set. Nothing resembling this exists in the repo.

text: [CRITICAL] "hERG IC50 > 50 μM (0% Risk)" — a 0% risk statement is never defensible, and the repo contains no exposure data, so the hERG safety margin that actually determines risk cannot be computed at all — Three distinct errors. (a) "0% Risk" is a claim of certainty. No assay and no model yields zero risk; a hERG assay yields a concentration-response with a confidence interval, and a hERG model yields a probability. (b) hERG risk is not an IC50, it is a ratio. The convention is margin = hERG IC50 / free plasma Cmax. The repo reports the numerator and contains no denominator anywhere — I grepped every platform file for dose, route, Cmax, AUC, clearance, half-life and plasma concentration and found zero hits. With IC50 = 50 μM, a 30x legacy margin permits free Cmax up to 1.67 μM (8.24 mg/L for a 4943 Da peptide); the ROC-optimal 37x TdP threshold permits 1.35 μM (6.68 mg/L); the 50x QTc threshold permits 1.00 μM (4.94 mg/L). Whether these candidates clear those bars is unknown and unknowable from this repo. (c) The value is reported to a single significant figure with a ">" and no CI, and is byte-identical across 25 different molecules ranging from an 8-residue peptide to a 100-residue construct with different natural-product warheads — physically impossible as a measurement or a prediction. Consequence: An expert reading "0% Risk" concludes cardiac safety has been cleared. Cardiac safety is the single most common cause of late-stage attrition and post-marketing withdrawal; ICH S7B/E14 require an integrated risk assessment, not an IC50. Publishing a zero-risk cardiotoxicity claim with no exposure term and no uncertainty is the exact pattern that produces false reassurance. It also poisons the rest of the safety panel by implying the same rigor was applied there.

text: Required fix for AIML-02: Remove "0% Risk" and "0% Cardiotoxicity" from README.md:99 and app.js:147 — no restatement of them is acceptable. Replace the hERG field with either (a) "Not assessed — out of applicability domain for small-molecule hERG models" for the peptide conjugates, or (b) if the small-molecule warhead alone is being assessed, a calibrated output of the form "P(hERG blocker) = 0.18, 90% conformal interval [0.06, 0.41], AD: in-domain (Tanimoto-to-training 0.42)" with the model, version and training set named. Add an explicit statement that no margin can be reported because no exposure (dose, route, free Cmax) has been estimated, and that a margin is required before any cardiac-safety claim.

text: Ground truth for AIML-02: Leishman, Abernathy & Wang (J Pharmacol Toxicol Methods 2020;105:106900, PMID 32768644) examined margins for 367 compounds against CredibleMeds TdP classes: mean margins were 4.8 (Known risk), 28 (Conditional), 71 (Possible) and 339 (Not listed); ROC-optimal thresholds were 37-fold for separating known-TdP from not-listed and 50-fold for QTc-positive vs QTc-negative — confirming the 2002 30-fold heuristic. Lehmann, Eggleston & Wang (Pharmacotherapy 2018;38:341-348, PMID 29380488) independently validated the hERG IC50:Cmax ratio against observed TdP incidence (correlation 0.312, 95% CI 0.205-0.476, p<0.0001). Modern ML hERG models output a calibrated probability of block with an interval and an applicability-domain verdict, not a binary clearance; conformal prediction is the standard way to attach guaranteed-coverage intervals (Alvarsson et al., J Pharm Sci 2021;110:42-49, PMID 33075380). Separately, note that every public hERG training set (e.g. the TDC hERG tasks used by ADMET-AI) contains small molecules of MW ~150-600; a 4943 Da polycationic peptide is categorically outside the applicability domain of all of them, so a model would have to abstain rather than return "safe".

text: [CRITICAL] The stated hERG mechanism is factually contradicted by the repo's own sequences, targets the wrong binding site for this modality, and ignores the one hERG route a polycationic peptide could actually take — The sentence is wrong three times over. (a) Its premise is false against its own data: every linker in the repo is a Gly-Ser linker (GGGGS or GGSGGS), the canonical *flexible hydrophilic* linker in fusion-protein engineering. Glycine and serine have Kyte-Doolittle values of -0.4 and -0.8; a GGGGS pentamer is among the least hydrophobic peptide segments constructible. There are no hydrophobic linkers in this platform. (b) The site named is the wrong one for the modality. Tyr652 and Phe656 sit on the S6 helices lining hERG's *inner* cavity, reached from the cytoplasmic face by small, lipophilic, typically basic amines that partition across the membrane. I computed GRAVY = -1.09 and net charge +8.98 at pH 7.4 for the 36-mer at app.js:153/247 — a strongly hydrophilic polycation of 4943 Da will not cross the plasma membrane and will never see Tyr652/Phe656. Arguing that a linker "sterically prevents" access to a site the molecule cannot reach in the first place is not a safety argument. (c) The route that *is* open to a polycationic peptide is the extracellular outer vestibule, and that is precisely the route the sentence does not address. Consequence: This is worse than an unsupported number: it is a mechanistic rationale that sounds authoritative and is verifiably false against the repo's own sequence data. A reader who checks the residues will conclude the author does not know how hERG block works; a reader who does not check will carry away a false mental model of why these molecules are safe. It also makes the "0% Risk" claim look like it was reasoned to rather than measured.

text: Required fix for AIML-03: Delete the mechanistic sentence at README.md:99 entirely. If a hERG statement is retained for the peptides, it must (a) name the outer-vestibule route as the plausible one, citing ErgTx/BeKm-1 precedent, (b) state that no extracellular hERG electrophysiology has been performed, and (c) list it as an open liability rather than a cleared one. Separately, correct any description of GGGGS as hydrophobic — it is the standard flexible hydrophilic linker.

tags: AI/ML for ADMET and toxicity property prediction — cheminformatics, computational safety pharmacology, model calibration and applicability domain
text: Ground truth for AIML-03: Tyr652/Phe656 are the classic inner-cavity aromatic determinants of high-affinity small-molecule hERG block (Ala-scanning of S6 and the pore helix; see e.g. Mitcheson-type SAR literature). Peptides block hERG by an entirely different route: ErgTx binds the *outer* vestibule formed by the S5-P and P-S6 linkers, with cysteine-scanning identifying Trp585, Gly590, Ile593 and Pro632 as the critical positions (Pardo-Lopez et al., J Biol Chem 2002;277:16403-16411, PMID 11864985). BeKm-1, a 36-residue scorpion toxin, blocks hERG at low-nM potency through the outer mouth, and its activity depends on an indispensable arginine (Arg20) forming a salt bridge and hydrogen bonds with the channel vestibule — replacing it even with lysine dramatically reduces block (Zavarzina et al., FEBS Lett 2024;598:889-901, PMID 38563123). In other words: a ~4-5 kDa arginine-rich peptide is exactly the chemotype known to block hERG from the outside. The relevant assay is therefore an extracellular-application patch-clamp on hERG (and, given the polycation, a broader Kv/Nav/Cav panel), not a Tyr652/Phe656 docking argument.

text: [CRITICAL] "Seizure Index = 0.01-0.02 / 1.0" is a fabricated metric — no such standardized index exists, and the best validated seizure-liability screens available reach only ~65% accuracy — There is no standardized, published, validated 0-to-1 "Seizure Index" in preclinical safety pharmacology. I searched for one and found nothing of the kind; what exists are MEA-based in vitro seizure liability assays reporting multi-parameter electrophysiological fingerprints, and ion-channel panels reporting per-target IC30/EC30 values — neither collapses to a single normalized scalar. The values here are reported to two decimal places (0.00 / 0.01 / 0.02) with no units, no scale definition, no reference compounds, no assay, and only three distinct values across 21 molecules. Compounding the error, the reported near-zero values are asserted for molecules whose declared pharmacology is squarely proconvulsant: NMDAR GluN2A modulation (app.js:215-220), α7 nAChR potentiation (app.js:195-200), M1 muscarinic PAM activity with explicit M-current suppression and increased burst firing (app.js:257-262), and AChE inhibition claimed to raise synaptic ACh by +350% (app.js:252). Cholinergic overdrive and M-current block are textbook seizurogenic mechanisms. The mitigating claim at app.js:219 and README.md:100 — "Capped Emax 135%" — is itself an unsupported number: an Emax requires a fitted concentration-response curve, and no dose-response data exists in the repo. Consequence: CNS drugs are killed by seizure liability, and seizure is among the most severe FDA black-box neurotoxicity warnings. Presenting a precise-looking scalar near zero for a portfolio built entirely on cholinergic and glutamatergic amplification inverts the actual risk signal: the pharmacology described is the pharmacology that causes convulsions. An expert reading this sees a fabricated reassurance placed exactly where the highest concern should be flagged.

text: Required fix for AIML-04: Delete "Seizure Index" from README.md:100 and all 21 app.js rows — it is not a real metric and cannot be repaired by rescaling. Replace with an honest qualitative risk statement that reflects the declared pharmacology: flag every AChE-inhibitor, α7 nAChR PAM, M1 PAM and NMDAR-modulating candidate as *elevated* seizure concern pending assay. If a quantitative claim is wanted, run the Cohen-style ion-channel panel or an hiPSC-neuron MEA assay and report per-target IC30/EC30 with the panel's published sensitivity/specificity attached to any resulting call. Delete "Capped Emax 135%" unless a fitted concentration-response curve with the fit parameters is committed alongside it.

tags: AI/ML for ADMET and toxicity property prediction — cheminformatics, computational safety pharmacology, model calibration and applicability domain
text: Ground truth for AIML-04: State of the art is (i) in vitro MEA-based seizure liability assays on rodent cortical or hiPSC-derived neuronal networks, scored on multi-parameter spike-train fingerprints against known seizurogenic and negative controls (Bradley et al., Toxicol Sci 2018;163:240-253, PMID 29432603), and (ii) automated-electrophysiology ion-channel panels. The performance ceiling is modest and must be stated: Cohen et al. (Toxicol Sci 2025;203:253-268, PMID 39661496) evaluated an 11-target panel (Cav2.1, Cav3.2, GlyRA1, AMPA, HCN1, Kv1.1, Kv7.2/7.3, NaV1.1, NaV1.2, GABA-A, NMDA) against 34 preclinical compounds and 45 approved drugs; the integrated panel predicted convulsion in nonclinical species with sensitivity 68%, specificity 56% and accuracy 65%, with Cav2.1 the single most informative target. A field whose best integrated assay reaches 65% accuracy cannot support a per-compound scalar reported to 0.01 resolution.

tags: AI/ML for ADMET and toxicity property prediction — cheminformatics, computational safety pharmacology, model calibration and applicability domain
text: [CRITICAL] "Tolerance Downregulation < 4.2% after 30 days" cannot be produced by any in-silico method, and the biased-agonism/recycling-endosome rationale offered for it has none of the measurements it requires — A 30-day receptor-downregulation percentage is a chronic in vivo pharmacodynamic endpoint. It requires repeated dosing in an animal over 30 days followed by receptor quantification at multiple timepoints — radioligand binding Bmax, cell-surface biotinylation, or quantitative immunoblot/immunohistochemistry in the target region — plus a matched vehicle arm. No simulation, docking score, or structure prediction produces this number; the repo contains no dosing regimen, no route, no species, no PK model, and no receptor-density data. Reporting it to one decimal place (4.2%, 3.5%, 3.8%) implies a measured mean. The proffered mechanism is equally unsupported: "biased agonist signaling redirects receptors to recycling endosomes" is a claim that requires, at minimum, (i) a quantified bias factor — ΔΔlog(τ/K_A) from the Black-Leff operational model fitted to at least two pathways against a reference agonist, (ii) β-arrestin recruitment assays (BRET/enzyme complementation) alongside the G-protein readout, and (iii) direct trafficking assays distinguishing Rab11-positive recycling from Rab7/lysosomal degradation. None of these appears anywhere. Separately, app.js:157 assigns "Tolerance Rate: 0.0%" to HippoAChE-AlkaPept-X2, whose declared mechanism (app.js:158) is enzyme inhibition of AChE plus blockade of Aβ fibrillogenesis — there is no receptor for it to downregulate, so the endpoint is not merely unmeasured, it is inapplicable. Consequence: Tolerance is the make-or-break question for any chronic cognitive-enhancement agent — it is why cholinesterase inhibitors and nicotinic agonists have disappointing durability. Presenting a sub-5% 30-day figure claims the field's central failure mode has been solved, on the basis of nothing. A reader deciding whether this approach is worth pursuing would be materially misled about the single most important risk to its thesis.

tags: AI/ML for ADMET and toxicity property prediction — cheminformatics, computational safety pharmacology, model calibration and applicability domain
text: Required fix for AIML-05: Delete the numeric downregulation claims at README.md:102, app.js:147, app.js:157 and app.js:187, and delete the biased-agonism sentence. Replace with "Not assessed — requires chronic in vivo dosing and receptor quantification." If the biased-signalling hypothesis is to be retained as a *hypothesis*, state it as such and specify the experiments that would test it: dual-pathway concentration-response (G-protein and β-arrestin) with operational-model bias factors and 95% CIs, plus Rab11 vs Rab7 colocalization trafficking assays. Remove the tolerance field entirely from non-receptor targets such as the AChE inhibitors (app.js:157).

tags: AI/ML for ADMET and toxicity property prediction — cheminformatics, computational safety pharmacology, model calibration and applicability domain
text: Ground truth for AIML-05: Ligand bias must be quantified, not asserted: the accepted framework is the operational model applied per pathway with subsequent calculation of ΔΔlogR / ΔΔlog(τ/K_A) relative to a reference agonist, and the field has repeatedly shown that apparent bias is assay-, cell- and system-dependent. The link from biased signalling to tolerance runs through measured trafficking: work on delta-opioid receptor agonists established that agonist-specific *recycling*, not internalization per se, tracks with tolerance liability (e.g. differential association of receptor-Gβγ complexes with β-arrestin2 determining recycling bias, PMC6620903; ligand- and cell-dependent determinants of DOR internalization, PMC3952036). Chronic receptor downregulation itself is measured in vivo, not predicted. No published in-silico method outputs a percentage downregulation at a 30-day horizon.

tags: AI/ML for ADMET and toxicity property prediction — cheminformatics, computational safety pharmacology, model calibration and applicability domain
text: [CRITICAL] "Low Immunogenicity" is asserted for 4-11 kDa foreign peptides with zero epitope analysis, and the justification offered conflates innate TLR4 signalling with adaptive anti-drug-antibody risk — Three problems. (a) No immunogenicity analysis was performed. The repo contains no MHC-II binding prediction, no T-cell epitope map, no ADA assessment. The scale of what is being waved through: the 36-mer at app.js:153/247 presents 22 overlapping 15-mer frames, all 22 of which contain a large hydrophobic residue (F/W/Y/L/I/V/M) in positions 1-6 and are therefore candidate P1-anchored MHC-II binders; the 100-mer at app.js:125 presents 86 frames, 53 of them with a candidate P1 anchor. Multiplied across HLA-DR, -DQ and -DP and their allotypes, "Low" is a verdict rendered over thousands of unscored peptide-allele pairs. (b) The two categories are conflated. "Cytokine Storm Potential" (innate, PRR-driven) and "Immunogenicity" (adaptive, MHC-II/CD4 T-cell-driven, producing anti-drug antibodies) are different mechanisms with different assays; suppressing TLR4/MD2 signalling does nothing to reduce MHC-II presentation of the drug's *own* sequence. The sentence at README.md:101 uses the second as evidence for the first. (c) The specific antigen chosen is the worst possible case for this claim. Candidate B4 (app.js:277) and AF3 candidate rank 5 (app.js:129) both present KLVFFAEDVGSNKGAIIGLM — Aβ16-35 — as the therapeutic payload. Deliberately administering an Aβ epitope to elderly patients is not a low-immunogenicity proposition; it is the design that caused the AN1792 program to be abandoned. Consequence: ADA formation against peptide therapeutics reduces exposure, abolishes efficacy, and in a minority of cases causes hypersensitivity or anaphylaxis. Regulators expect an in-silico immunogenicity risk assessment as a routine step in the development path for biologics. Asserting "Low" without one — and doing so for a construct built around an Aβ autoantigen — would be flagged immediately by any biologics development group and undermines confidence in the whole safety panel.

tags: AI/ML for ADMET and toxicity property prediction — cheminformatics, computational safety pharmacology, model calibration and applicability domain
text: Required fix for AIML-06: Remove all "Low/Very Low Immunogenicity" and "Cytokine Storm Risk: 0%/None" strings (README.md:101; app.js:167, 271, 303, 323, 343). Separate the two endpoints into distinct fields — innate/PRR activation and adaptive ADA risk — because they require different evidence. Run NetMHCIIpan-4.3 over every candidate sequence against a representative HLA-DR/DQ/DP panel, commit the raw per-frame scores, and report a hit-count-based risk tier with the allele coverage stated. Flag the Aβ16-35-containing candidates (app.js:277, app.js:129) as carrying a specific, precedented CNS autoimmune risk and cite AN1792.

tags: AI/ML for ADMET and toxicity property prediction — cheminformatics, computational safety pharmacology, model calibration and applicability domain
text: Ground truth for AIML-06: The standard workflow is: (1) exhaustive 15-mer sliding-window scoring against a broad HLA class II allele panel using NetMHCIIpan-4.3, which closes the accuracy gap across DR, DQ and DP loci using immunopeptidomics-trained ML (Nilsson et al., Sci Adv 2023;9:eadj6367, PMID 38000035); (2) epitope-cluster and regulatory-T-cell analysis, e.g. the EpiMatrix / ClustiMer / JanusMatrix pipeline, which additionally scores human homology and Treg-epitope content and is explicitly supported for peptide drugs (Mattei et al., mAbs 2024;16:2333729, PMID 38536724); (3) confirmatory ex vivo human PBMC / CD4 T-cell proliferation or HLA-DR-restricted assays; (4) a stated ADA risk category. On the Aβ payload specifically: in the Phase IIa AN1792 trial of active Aβ42 immunization, 6% of vaccinated patients developed meningoencephalitis and the program was abandoned (reviewed in Yang & Xiao, Curr Pharm Biotechnol 2015;16:484-491, PMID 25860060; also Panza et al., Curr Alzheimer Res 2011;8:808-817, PMID 21592055).

text: [CRITICAL] The liabilities that actually govern this modality — membrane lysis/hemolysis, mammalian cytotoxicity, aggregation, proteolytic instability, polypharmacology — are absent entirely, while an inapplicable liability (hERG) is reported for all 25 — These sequences are cationic amphipathic peptides — the antimicrobial/cell-penetrating chemotype — and the platform reports none of the liabilities that define that class. My calculations (average residue masses; Eisenberg consensus hydrophobicity; α-helical 100°/residue moment; Henderson-Hasselbalch net charge at pH 7.4): KWWKFLRRFWRR (README.md:74) is 1865 Da, q = +5.99, μH = 0.989; FLRRFWRR (README.md:64) is 1237 Da, q = +3.99, μH = 1.068; the 36-mer at app.js:153/247 is 4943 Da, q = +8.98, 13 Lys+Arg vs 4 Asp+Glu, μH = 0.615. For calibration I ran the same code on reference lytic peptides: melittin μH = 0.353, LL-37 μH = 0.559, TAT(47-57) q = +7.99. The candidate peptides are as amphipathic as, or more amphipathic than, the canonical membrane-lytic references. Trp/Arg-rich cationic 8-12-mers of exactly this composition are a well-characterized engineered-AMP series. Yet the safety field for these molecules reports hERG (largely inapplicable, see AIML-03) and a fabricated Seizure Index, and is silent on: hemolysis (HC50 against human erythrocytes), mammalian cytotoxicity (HepG2/HEK293/primary neurons and astrocytes), off-target polypharmacology (polycations bind heparan sulfate proteoglycans, phosphatidylserine, nucleic acids and anionic membranes indiscriminately), peptide self-aggregation, and plasma/CSF proteolytic stability. I want to be precise rather than alarmist: this chemotype is not uniformly toxic — Deslouches et al. found WK12 and WR12 to have negligible hemolytic and cytotoxic effects up to 10x MIC — which is exactly the point. Whether a given cationic amphipathic peptide is lytic depends on charge, hydrophobicity, length and amphipathicity in ways that must be measured. It cannot be asserted, and it certainly cannot be inferred from a hERG number. Consequence: The safety panel is calibrated for the wrong modality. It reports the liability of small-molecule CNS drugs (hERG, seizure) for molecules that are peptides, and omits every liability specific to peptides. A reader comparing candidates on this panel is comparing them on axes that do not discriminate, while the axes that would discriminate — lysis, cytotoxicity, stability, aggregation — are invisible. For CNS delivery this is compounded: peptides of 4-5 kDa with strongly negative GRAVY do not cross the blood-brain barrier and are rapidly degraded in plasma, so even the efficacy premise is untested; but the immediate safety consequence is that a potentially hemolytic polycation is being presented with a clean bill of health.

text: Required fix for AIML-07: Add the peptide panel above as explicit fields in the data model, populated with "Not assessed" until measured — an honest gap is a scientific statement; an omitted liability is not. Simultaneously mark hERG as "Not applicable / out of domain" for the peptide conjugates rather than reporting a clean value. Compute and display, at no experimental cost, the sequence-derived descriptors that already flag the risk: length, MW, net charge at pH 7.4, GRAVY, and Eisenberg hydrophobic moment, with the melittin/LL-37 reference values shown for calibration. Add BBB penetration and plasma stability as open questions in README.md Section 3.

tags: AI/ML for ADMET and toxicity property prediction — cheminformatics, computational safety pharmacology, model calibration and applicability domain
text: Ground truth for AIML-07: For a cationic amphipathic peptide the obligatory developability/safety panel is: (1) hemolysis — HC50 on fresh human RBCs, reported alongside the efficacious concentration as a therapeutic index; (2) mammalian cytotoxicity — MTT/LDH on at least one hepatic, one renal and one target-tissue primary line; (3) plasma and CSF proteolytic stability — t1/2 in human plasma and brain homogenate; (4) aggregation propensity — sequence-based predictors (TANGO/WALTZ/AGGRESCAN class) plus ThT and DLS; (5) off-target polypharmacology — at minimum a broad receptor/ion-channel safety panel plus heparin/PS binding, because polycations are promiscuous; (6) BBB permeability and route. Deslouches et al. (J Med Microbiol 2016;65:554-565, PMID 27046192) is the reference showing both that Trp/Arg 12-mers of this exact composition are potent membrane permeabilizers and that hemolysis must be assayed rather than assumed, since their WK12/WR12 series proved well tolerated up to 10x MIC while related sequences are not.

text: [CRITICAL] Two candidates use Aβ16-35 / Aβ16-23 verbatim as the therapeutic payload and are labelled "Aβ Disruptor" with "Fibril Blockade: 100%" — the sequence used is one of the shortest known amyloid-*forming* fragments of Aβ, i.e. a seed, not a breaker — I aligned the payload against Aβ42 (DAEFRHDSGYEVHHQKLVFFAEDVGSNKGAIIGLMVGGVVIA): "KLVFFAEDVGSNKGAIIGLM" is an exact match to residues 16-35, and "KLVFFAED" at README.md:77 is an exact match to residues 16-23. This is not an Aβ-derived inhibitor scaffold; it is a verbatim copy of the Aβ central hydrophobic cluster (KLVFFA, 16-21) *plus* the second hydrophobic region (GAIIGLM, 29-35) — the two segments that drive Aβ self-assembly. Aβ16-22 in isolation forms highly ordered antiparallel cross-β amyloid fibrils on its own. My physicochemical numbers are consistent: the B4 payload has GRAVY +0.26 and net charge +1.03, i.e. a near-neutral hydrophobic peptide, the regime that favors β-sheet self-assembly, in contrast to every other candidate in the portfolio. Administering this into a brain that already contains Aβ plaques is a seeding proposition. Labelling it a "Fibril Disruptor" with "Fibril Blockade: 100%" (app.js:281) inverts the direction of the effect, and "100%" is a fabricated completeness claim on top of it. Note also that the aggregation liability is invisible to the platform's safety panel, which for this molecule reports only hERG, Seizure Index 0.01, and the 100% fibril figure. Consequence: This is the single most dangerous design error in the portfolio, because it is directionally wrong rather than merely unsupported: the molecule proposed as a therapy is the fragment used experimentally to *nucleate* amyloid. A reader who takes the label at face value would pursue a construct whose most likely in vivo effect on the stated endpoint is the opposite of the intended one. It also carries the immunogenicity precedent from AIML-06 — dosing an Aβ epitope into elderly patients has a documented history of CNS adverse events.

text: Required fix for AIML-08: Withdraw both candidates (app.js:275-282 and app.js:129) or redesign the payload. If an Aβ-recognition element is genuinely wanted, replace the wild-type CHC with a register-disrupted analogue (proline or N-methyl substitution within LVFFA, or a D-enantiomer/retro-inverso backbone) and say explicitly which modification confers the breaker activity. Remove "Fibril Blockade: 100%" (app.js:281). Add aggregation propensity — sequence predictor plus ThT kinetics and seeded-aggregation assay against recombinant Aβ42 — as a mandatory safety endpoint for any candidate containing an amyloidogenic segment, and flag the Aβ16-35 payload as a seeding risk in README.md:77.

tags: AI/ML for ADMET and toxicity property prediction — cheminformatics, computational safety pharmacology, model calibration and applicability domain
text: Ground truth for AIML-08: Balbach, Ishii, Antzutkin, Leapman, Rizzo, Dyda, Reed & Tycko (Biochemistry 2000;39:13748-13759, PMID 11076514) established by EM, X-ray powder diffraction, birefringence and solid-state 13C NMR that Ac-KLVFFAE-NH2 (Aβ16-22) forms genuine amyloid fibrils with a β-strand backbone extending from Leu17 through Ala21 and an antiparallel β-sheet organization, and describe it as "among the shortest fibril-forming fragments of full-length β-amyloid reported to date". Subsequent work confirmed the same for the uncapped peptide and mapped the assembly pathway (e.g. PMID 21309606, PMID 35134456). Peptides that actually *break* Aβ β-sheets are deliberately register-disrupted derivatives of the CHC — proline substitution, N-methylation, or D-amino acid backbones — not wild-type copies; the β-sheet-breaker literature is explicit that the disrupting modification, not the recognition sequence, provides the activity.

text: [MAJOR] No safety value in the platform carries uncertainty, an applicability-domain verdict, a model identity, or provenance — the four things that make a prediction usable — Every safety and affinity figure is a bare point estimate. There is no confidence interval, no standard error, no probability, no prediction set, no coverage level. There is no applicability-domain statement anywhere — critical here because the entities being scored (4-11 kDa polycationic peptides) fall outside the training distribution of every public small-molecule ADMET model. There is no model name, version, training set, or hyperparameter record. There is no timestamp, no git SHA, no input manifest. Structurally, the safety field also has no schema: I extracted the third endpoint slot across the 25 rows and found 22 distinct labels (Downregulation, Tolerance Rate, Tolerance Downregulation, Immunogenicity, Tumorigenicity, Receptor Desensitization, Desensitization, Off-target Binding, Excitotoxicity, Systemic Toxicity, Peripheral Side Effects, Fibril Blockade, Safety Plasticity Score, Safety Index, Sepsis Safety, Cytokine Storm Risk, Inflammatory Cytokine Suppression, Lysosomal Clearance, Vasodilation Rate, Glutamate Toxicity, Tau Hyperphosphorylation, Cerebral Edema, Edema Risk), so no two candidates report the same endpoint set and cross-candidate ranking on safety is impossible. Several of those labels are efficacy claims (Lysosomal Clearance +420%, Inflammatory Cytokine Suppression 98%, Vasodilation Rate +45%, Tau Hyperphosphorylation Suppressed) presented under a heading that says "ADMET Safety Profile & Side Effects". Consequence: Even if a real model were wired in tomorrow, a point estimate with no uncertainty and no domain check is not decision-grade — it is the failure mode that causes silent, confident errors on out-of-domain inputs, which is precisely the regime these molecules occupy. And the heterogeneous schema means the panel cannot serve its one legitimate purpose, which is comparing 25 candidates on a common safety axis.

tags: AI/ML for ADMET and toxicity property prediction — cheminformatics, computational safety pharmacology, model calibration and applicability domain
text: Required fix for AIML-09: Define one fixed safety schema applied identically to all 25 candidates: {endpoint, value, uncertainty (interval + coverage level), model, model version, training set, applicability-domain verdict, date, git SHA} — with "not assessed" as a first-class allowed value. Wrap whatever model is adopted in inductive conformal prediction at a stated confidence level (90% is conventional) and render the interval, not just the point. Add an explicit AD check (e.g. maximum Tanimoto or embedding distance to the training set) and force abstention when out of domain rather than returning a value. Move all efficacy-flavored fields (Lysosomal Clearance, Cytokine Suppression, Vasodilation Rate, Tau Hyperphosphorylation, Fibril Blockade) out of the safety panel into an efficacy panel.

tags: AI/ML for ADMET and toxicity property prediction — cheminformatics, computational safety pharmacology, model calibration and applicability domain
text: Ground truth for AIML-09: Conformal prediction is the standard, model-agnostic way to attach validity guarantees: it retrofits any QSAR model into a confidence predictor emitting prediction intervals (regression) or prediction sets (classification) at a user-specified confidence level, with error-rate guarantees and an applicability domain that is intrinsically linked to the underlying model (Alvarsson, Arvidsson McShane, Norinder & Spjuth, J Pharm Sci 2021;110:42-49, PMID 33075380; the framing of conformal prediction as an OECD-principles-compliant alternative to ad hoc AD definitions goes back to Norinder et al. 2014). Chemprop v1/v2 ship uncertainty quantification and calibration methods with the relevant metrics built in (Heid et al., J Chem Inf Model 2024;64:9-17, PMID 38147829). ADMET-AI (PMID 38913862) additionally contextualizes each prediction against a DrugBank reference percentile, which is the minimum interpretability affordance a portfolio panel should offer.

text: [MINOR] Safety profiles are generated for inputs that are not sequences and for sequences containing non-standard residues, proving no validation layer touched the data — Candidate A4's `sequence` field contains the English string "His14-Phe174-Linker-Peptide-Conjugate", not a peptide sequence, yet it is assigned a complete ADMET profile at app.js:385 ("hERG IC50 > 50 μM | Seizure Index: 0.00 | Cerebral Edema: Prevented") and is passed unchecked into initModal3DCanvas, renderModalPlddtChart and renderModalPaeHeatmap, which will index it character-by-character and render a "pLDDT profile" for the letters in the word "Linker". Separately, three sequences contain the character `B`, which is the IUPAC ambiguity code for Asx (Asn/Asp) and is not a standard amino acid; AlphaFold Server would reject it, so these sequences demonstrably never went through the pipeline the platform claims. This is a small defect on its own but it is the cleanest available proof for AIML-01: a data set in which a prose string and an invalid residue code both pass through to a rendered safety profile has no validation layer, and therefore no pipeline. Consequence: It removes any remaining ambiguity about whether some upstream computation might have existed and merely been cached as strings. It also means the FASTA copy button (index.html:362) will hand a user an unsubmittable sequence for at least four candidates, wasting their time at the AlphaFold Server.

text: Ground truth for AIML-10: Any sequence-consuming pipeline validates its input first: alphabet restricted to the 20 standard one-letter codes (with an explicit policy for B/Z/X/U/O), non-empty, length within model limits, and a hard failure — not a rendered chart — on violation. AlphaFold Server accepts only standard residues for protein chains.

tags: AI/ML for ADMET and toxicity property prediction — cheminformatics, computational safety pharmacology, model calibration and applicability domain
text: ADMET-AI: a machine learning ADMET platform for evaluation of large-scale chemical libraries (2024). Open-source, locally runnable Chemprop-based ADMET prediction across the TDC endpoint suite (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, toxicity including hERG), with DrugBank-referenced percentile context; highest average rank on the TDC ADMET Leaderboard; one million molecules in 3.1 h locally. Application here: This is the drop-in replacement for the 25 hardcoded strings, for the small-molecule natural-product warheads (Huperzine A, curcumin, baicalein, asiatic acid, ginkgolide B, ferulic acid). Run it from a committed script over the warhead SMILES, emit JSON per compound, and have app.js read that JSON. It will NOT cover the peptide conjugates — its training data is small molecules — which is itself the finding to report for those entries.

tags: AI/ML for ADMET and toxicity property prediction — cheminformatics, computational safety pharmacology, model calibration and applicability domain
text: Therapeutics Data Commons: Machine Learning Datasets and Tasks for Drug Discovery and Development (2021). The benchmark substrate for therapeutic ML: 66 AI-ready datasets across 22 learning tasks, including the ADMET benchmark group (hERG, CYP inhibition, Caco-2, BBB, clearance, LD50, DILI) with fixed scaffold splits and leaderboards. Application here: Use the TDC ADMET benchmark group to establish what performance any adopted model actually achieves on each endpoint, and quote that performance next to every prediction shown in the UI. It also supplies the honest counterargument to the hERG claims: the hERG training sets are small molecules of MW ~150-600, so a 4.9 kDa peptide is out of domain and the model must abstain.

tags: AI/ML for ADMET and toxicity property prediction — cheminformatics, computational safety pharmacology, model calibration and applicability domain
text: Chemprop: A Machine Learning Package for Chemical Property Prediction (2024). Reference D-MPNN implementation with built-in uncertainty quantification and calibration methods, transfer learning, and hyperparameter optimization; the model layer underneath ADMET-AI. Application here: Use Chemprop's UQ/calibration facilities so every predicted safety endpoint ships with a calibrated uncertainty rather than a bare point value, directly remediating AIML-09. Pin the version and commit the trained checkpoint hash.

tags: AI/ML for ADMET and toxicity property prediction — cheminformatics, computational safety pharmacology, model calibration and applicability domain
text: Predicting With Confidence: Using Conformal Prediction in Drug Discovery (2021). Practical introduction to conformal prediction as a model-agnostic layer producing prediction intervals (regression) and prediction sets (classification) with guaranteed error rates, and an applicability domain intrinsically linked to the underlying model — satisfying the OECD (Q)SAR principles. Application here: Wrap whichever ADMET model is adopted in inductive conformal prediction at a stated confidence level (e.g. 90%), so the UI shows 'P(hERG blocker) = 0.18, 90% CP interval [0.06, 0.41], AD: out-of-domain' instead of '0% Risk'. This is the single change that would move the safety panel from indefensible to defensible.

tags: AI/ML for ADMET and toxicity property prediction — cheminformatics, computational safety pharmacology, model calibration and applicability domain
text: Revisiting the hERG safety margin after 20 years of routine hERG screening (2020). Empirical re-derivation of the hERG safety margin across 367 compounds: mean IC50/free-Cmax margins of 4.8 (Known TdP risk), 28 (Conditional), 71 (Possible) and 339 (Not listed); ROC-optimal thresholds of 37-fold (TdP) and 50-fold (QTc), confirming the 2002 30-fold heuristic. Application here: This is the ground truth against which 'hERG IC50 > 50 μM (0% Risk)' fails: risk is the ratio, not the numerator. Use it to state explicitly that with IC50 = 50 μM the free Cmax must stay below ~1.35 μM (37x) for the TdP margin to be met, and that the repo contains no exposure estimate at all.

tags: AI/ML for ADMET and toxicity property prediction — cheminformatics, computational safety pharmacology, model calibration and applicability domain
text: Validation and Clinical Utility of the hERG IC50:Cmax Ratio to Determine the Risk of Drug-Induced Torsades de Pointes: A Meta-Analysis (2018). Independent meta-analytic validation that the hERG IC50:free-Cmax ratio correlates with observed TdP incidence (0.312, 95% CI 0.205-0.476, p<0.0001), with a negligible-risk ratio around 80. Application here: Second, independent source establishing that the margin — not the IC50 — is the risk metric, and that risk is expressed as a graded incidence correlation, never as '0%'. Cite alongside Leishman when rewriting README.md:99.

tags: AI/ML for ADMET and toxicity property prediction — cheminformatics, computational safety pharmacology, model calibration and applicability domain
text: In vitro human ion channel assays predictive of drug-induced seizure (2025). Evaluation of an 11-target ion-channel panel (Cav2.1, Cav3.2, GlyRA1, AMPA, HCN1, Kv1.1, Kv7.2/7.3, NaV1.1, NaV1.2, GABA-A, NMDA) by automated electrophysiology against 34 preclinical compounds and 45 approved drugs; the integrated panel predicts convulsion with sensitivity 68%, specificity 56%, accuracy 65%; Cav2.1 the most informative single target. Application here: This is the performance ceiling that makes 'Seizure Index = 0.01/1.0' indefensible: the best integrated seizure screen in the field reaches 65% accuracy, so no method supports a per-compound scalar at 0.01 resolution. It also specifies the panel to actually run on the α7 nAChR, GluN2A, M1 and AChE-inhibitor candidates.

tags: AI/ML for ADMET and toxicity property prediction — cheminformatics, computational safety pharmacology, model calibration and applicability domain
text: In Vitro Screening for Seizure Liability Using Microelectrode Array Technology (2018). MEA-based seizure liability screen on cryopreserved rat cortical neurons, scoring 12 spike-train parameters against 20 reference compounds spanning GABA-A antagonists, glycine receptor antagonists, ion channel blockers and muscarinic agonists; 16/17 seizurogenic or neurotoxic compounds detected. Application here: The accepted new-approach methodology for seizure liability, and the concrete assay to substitute for the invented Seizure Index. Note that its readout is a multi-parameter fingerprint against reference compounds, not a normalized scalar — which is exactly why the platform's metric does not exist.

tags: AI/ML for ADMET and toxicity property prediction — cheminformatics, computational safety pharmacology, model calibration and applicability domain
text: Accurate prediction of HLA class II antigen presentation across all loci using tailored data acquisition and refined machine learning (NetMHCIIpan-4.3) (2023). Current state-of-the-art pan-allele MHC class II binding/presentation predictor with closed performance gap across HLA-DR, -DQ and -DP, trained on large immunopeptidomics datasets and accommodating inverted binding modes. Application here: Run over every candidate sequence as exhaustive 15-mer sliding windows against a representative DR/DQ/DP allele panel — 22 frames for the 36-mer at app.js:153, 86 for the 100-mer at app.js:125 — and replace 'Low Immunogenicity' with a hit-count-based risk tier and committed raw scores.

tags: AI/ML for ADMET and toxicity property prediction — cheminformatics, computational safety pharmacology, model calibration and applicability domain
text: In silico methods for immunogenicity risk assessment and human homology screening for therapeutic antibodies (2024). Description of the ISPRI immunogenicity workflow — EpiMatrix epitope mapping, ClustiMer clustering, JanusMatrix human-homology/Treg-epitope analysis, OptiMatrix deimmunization — with normalized immunogenicity scoring, explicitly supported for peptide drugs as well as antibodies. Application here: Supplies the second half of a credible ADA risk assessment beyond raw MHC-II binding: epitope clustering, human-homology screening, and a normalized comparative immunogenicity score. Directly applicable to the Aβ16-35-containing candidates at app.js:277 and app.js:129, where human homology is the specific concern.

tags: AI/ML for ADMET and toxicity property prediction — cheminformatics, computational safety pharmacology, model calibration and applicability domain
text: Amyloid fibril formation by A beta 16-22, a seven-residue fragment of the Alzheimer's beta-amyloid peptide, and structural characterization by solid state NMR (2000). Definitive demonstration by EM, X-ray powder diffraction, birefringence and solid-state 13C NMR that Ac-KLVFFAE-NH2 forms ordered antiparallel cross-β amyloid fibrils on its own, with β-strand conformation from Leu17 through Ala21; described as among the shortest fibril-forming fragments of full-length Aβ. Application here: Establishes that the payload of BasalAChE-Abeta-B4 (app.js:277, Aβ16-35) and AF3 candidate rank 5 (app.js:129) is an amyloid seed, not an amyloid disruptor, falsifying the 'Fibril Blockade: 100%' claim at app.js:281 and the 'Aβ Disruptor' label at README.md:77.

tags: AI/ML for ADMET and toxicity property prediction — cheminformatics, computational safety pharmacology, model calibration and applicability domain
text: Comparative functional properties of engineered cationic antimicrobial peptides consisting exclusively of tryptophan and either lysine or arginine (2016). Systematic characterization of engineered Trp/Arg and Trp/Lys cationic peptides of 8-18 residues: membrane permeabilization by SPR and flow cytometry, plus hemolytic and tetrazolium cytotoxicity assays; WK12/WR12 showed negligible hemolysis up to 10x MIC while shorter/other analogues differ. Application here: Defines the assay set missing from the platform for KWWKFLRRFWRR, FLRRFWRR and the 36-mer amphipathic helix (hemolysis HC50, mammalian cytotoxicity, membrane permeabilization), and supplies the calibrated caveat that this chemotype's lytic behaviour must be measured rather than assumed in either direction.

tags: AI/ML for ADMET and toxicity property prediction — cheminformatics, computational safety pharmacology, model calibration and applicability domain
text: Mapping the binding site of a human ether-a-go-go-related gene-specific peptide toxin (ErgTx) to the channel's outer vestibule (2002). Cysteine-scanning mutagenesis of the hERG S5-P and P-S6 linkers identifying Trp585, Gly590, Ile593 and Pro632 as the determinants of peptide-toxin binding at the channel's outer vestibule — a site and mechanism entirely distinct from small-molecule inner-cavity block at Tyr652/Phe656. Application here: Falsifies the mechanistic claim at README.md:99. If these polycationic peptides have any hERG liability it would be via the extracellular outer vestibule, which the platform's steric argument does not address; the corresponding assay is extracellular-application patch-clamp, not a Tyr652/Phe656 docking rationale.

tags: AI/ML for ADMET and toxicity property prediction — cheminformatics, computational safety pharmacology, model calibration and applicability domain
text: The scorpion toxin BeKm-1 blocks hERG cardiac potassium channels using an indispensable arginine residue (2024). MD and ensemble docking model of the hERG-BeKm-1 complex showing Arg20 of the 36-residue toxin forming a simultaneous salt bridge and hydrogen bonds with the channel vestibule; the R20K mutant shows dramatically reduced hERG activity. Application here: Direct counterexample to the implicit premise that a polycationic peptide cannot pose hERG risk: an arginine-rich ~4 kDa peptide is precisely the chemotype that blocks hERG at low nM, and it does so through an arginine. Cite when rewriting README.md:99 for the app.js:153/247 36-mer (q = +8.98, 13 K+R).

tags: AI/ML for ADMET and toxicity property prediction — cheminformatics, computational safety pharmacology, model calibration and applicability domain
text: New developments of clinical trial in immunotherapy for Alzheimer's disease (2015). Review documenting that in the Phase IIa AN1792 trial of active Aβ42 immunization, 6% of vaccinated patients developed meningoencephalitis as an adverse effect, leading to abandonment of the program (corroborated by Panza et al., Curr Alzheimer Res 2011;8:808-817, PMID 21592055). Application here: Clinical precedent falsifying 'Low Immunogenicity' for the Aβ-epitope-bearing candidates at app.js:277 and app.js:129. Any construct presenting Aβ16-35 to an elderly CNS population must carry an explicit CNS autoimmunity risk flag citing this history.
